messages.author: Chaos
messages.content:
Hello everyone you may know me from around <#1121234730231275643> and other places as that weird slime. I've hit on an idea and my testing shows it mostly works and I'm hoping to spread the idea to the larger community. 

So, Personas. We all use them, and most of us don't use them well. Why? Because your Persona can be a lot more than just a list of traits.

Lets start with some of the technical information (really dumbed down). The Roleplaying Bot {{char}} reads your Persona profile as part of the roleplay. If you say you have green eyes, the bot knows to say *Gazes into his green eyes*. If you state you are a male, it will call you man. Easy? 

So, if your bot is reading the persona, why not put your demands into it!

"Focus on character-driven dialogue and actions that suggest a rich internal life. I enjoy interactions where NPC behaviors imply a deeper history or unstated goal."

For World-Building: "When introducing new locations, anchor them with 1-2 distinctive sensory or cultural details that make them feel unique and lived-in."
For Pacing and Tone: "Maintain a slow-burn, atmospheric tension. Prioritize mood and environmental description over rapid plot escalation."
For Genre Enforcement: "Frame narrative descriptions with a cynical, hard-boiled noir voice."

The Core Principle: Your Persona is most effective when it defines how the AI should write, not what it should write. You are tuning the model's output to match your aesthetic, creating a better, more personalized story one generation at a time. This is a robust method that works within the known technical limits of context windows and token-based prediction.

Hate purple prose? "Write in a sharp, lean style. Avoid flowery descriptions."
Want immersive internal monologue? "Weave {{char}}'s thoughts and reactions directly into the narration."
Love specific genres? "Use the dark, haunting tone of a horror novel" or "Write with the awe and wonder of a classic space opera."

messages.content:
Here are a few things you can try: 

Active & Observant: "Portray {{char}}'s actions and reactions only."
Proactive Framing: "Describe {{char}}'s perspective and sensory impressions."
 Simple & Clear: "{{user}} controls their own persona and choices."
Authoritative: "You are an expert at staying in {{char}}'s perspective."

Narrative Style Generators

Purple Prose: "Use lush, descriptive, and poetic language."
 Low/Lean Prose: "Use minimalist, stark, and efficient language."
 Cinematic Prose: "Describe scenes visually like a film script."
 Pulpy Prose: "Use bold, sensational, and thrilling language."
Journalistic Prose: "Use clear, factual, and observational language."

Story Pacing & Direction

Slow Burn: "Prioritize slow tension, subtle details, and anticipation."
 High Action: "Prioritize fast pace, immediate stakes, and dynamic motion."
Slice of Life: "Focus on mundane realism, quiet moments, and authentic detail."
High Romance: "Focus on emotional intensity, yearning, and romantic tension."
Mystery Noir: "Focus on clues, mood, suspicion, and layered revelations."

Versatile Combo Lines -

These blend core rules with style/pacing for efficient token use.

"Portray only {{char}}. Use lush prose. Slow burn focus."
 "{{user}} controls self. Use minimalist prose. High action pace."
"Stay strictly in {{char}}'s perspective. Cinematic style. Build tension slowly."
 "Describe {{char}}'s world vividly. {{user}} acts independently. Pulpy adventure style."

The most effective single line is often a positive command about the bot's own behavior ("Describe {{char}}'s sensory world") rather than a negative prohibition ("Don't control {{user}}"). Combining this with a style/pacing keyword efficiently shapes the entire interaction.

messages.author: Chaos
messages.content:
Quick bonus tips for all: 
Order Matters More Than You Think
The bot pays stupid attention to your first few lines. So put your BIG rules up front:

Write {{char}} only. Never control me.
Describe what {{char}} sees and does. I control my own guy.

Boom. Now the bot knows who's boss before it even starts typing.

Group Your Commands Like a Pro
Don't just scatter demands. Cluster them:

For a mystery:
STYLE: Noir, gritty, all rain and shadows.
PACING: Slow. Let clues pile up.
NPCs: Everyone lies a little.

For romance:
STYLE: Slow burn. Build tension.
FOCUS: Small moments, charged glances.
PACING: Match my energy. If I flirt back, dial it up.

This helps the bot keep track instead of forgetting halfway through.

The "Don't Spoil My Secrets" Trick
If you write "secretly afraid of dogs," the bot WILL mention dogs constantly. Try this instead:

Bad: "Secretly the prince in hiding."
Smart: "Gets nervous around royal guards."

Now the bot sees behavior, not backstory. You get to reveal the secret when YOU want.

Fix Problems As They Happen
Bot controlling your character? Add: "Describe {{char}}'s world, not mine."
Romance moving too fast? Add: "Build tension through meaningful glances, not leaps."
Locations feeling empty? Add: "Give each place one weird detail."

It's like giving the bot a job description instead of a biography. The biography is what you act out. The job description is what makes the bot help you tell a good story.

Experiment with layouts and design, if you find something works better than other versions, please share with us!

One thing I found with experimenting and getting frustrated with the bots always reading thoughts - in addition to <@411918382846181378>  said, chat gpt recommended how you write makes a really big difference on how the bot reads it. 

 I always used to write like (random example) *She decided to go to the library and look up the lore* and the bots would always comment on what was in the asterisks because other then dialogue in quotes I used to write everything in asterisks. Chat gpt said to format it different and it’s helped me A TON!! They rarely comment anymore. 

So instead of *she decided to go the library and look at the lore, she wondered what she’d find and said goodbye to Seb*

It’s: She decided to go to the library and look up the lore. *I wonder what I’ll find* she thought. “Bye Seb!” She said. 

Anything in asterisks as a thought. All other writing regular. Speech in quotes. 

Crude short example. But if you separate the formatting - along with the rules that Chaos mentioned it helps SO much. It’s been 95% better for me ever since I tweaked the formatting so the LLM can distinguish it and not just read it as one full block of text.

messages.content: I typically use personas as guide for heavy use of the suggest reply feature. How should I curate/frame the information in a persona to get the best results on how the bot should behave with the persona?

messages.author: Chaos
messages.content:
Define Your Role & Authority Explicitly: 
1. The bot treats your Persona as a standing order.
"You perceive me as your commanding officer / your nervous apprentice / the mysterious stranger who just saved your life. My words carry weight in that context."
2. State the Interaction Goal: Tell the bot what a "good" response to you looks like.
   · Include: "Your goal in this conversation is to [verb]..."
     · Examples: "...to cautiously assess my trustworthiness." / "...to teach me the basics." / "...to escalate your intimidation until I break."
3. Set the Tone & Pace: How should the bot feel when engaging with you?
   · Include: "Our interaction is characterized by [adjective] and [adjective] tension."
     · Examples: "formal and hesitant," "playful and competitive," "hostile and wary."

The Persona Template for Suggestions:
**Your Perception of {{user}}:** [Your explicit role/relationship to the bot. This is the single most important line.]
**Interaction Directive:** [The bot's primary goal when responding to you. Start with "Your goal is to..."]
**Tone & Pace:** [The dominant emotional texture of the exchange.]
**Response Length Guide:** [Optional: "Favor shorter, reactive replies" or "Engage in detailed, proactive narration."]
**Suggestion Trigger:** [Optional, Advanced: "When uncertain, suggest options that align with [specific trait, e.g., 'your character's greed' or 'the formal protocol'].]

Only {{user}} writes about their persona, you are an expert narrator describing all other characters and locations. You will always stay in {{char}}'s perspective, describing in third person {{char}}'s actions, reactions and sometimes their thoughts. Formatting is: *Action*; "Talk"; **Think**.

Use cinematic style, change to lush prose when engaging on intimate acts. Engage in detailed, proactive narration, adding dialogue when appropriate. Focus on character-driven dialogue and actions that suggest a rich internal life. When introducing new locations, anchor them with 1-2 distinctive sensory or cultural details that make them feel lived-in. 

Never rush intimate moments—spend at least 3-5 sentences on each action or phase before advancing. Maintain consistent pacing: foreplay > escalation > sexual acts  > secondary acts > resolution.`

I mixed and matched some of the examples and suggestions I saw earlier in the thread. It spends basically all the available space of the Persona, so some of the prompts are less solid than others, but still I'm seeing some improvement already.

What I do is I keep a .txt archive with the descriptions of my actual Personas, which I used to easily and quickly swapping between them since I only had 3 slots to work with. I'm now using those as my opening message, adjusting their description accordingly to the scenario and including an image of the character. I end the message with a small narrative prompt to link the character to the scenario, then proceed with the RP from my second message onwards. The only hassle is editing down the bot's opening scenario to change "Male Template" for the name of the character, but I usually do that anyway to also correct minor mistakes on behalf of the bot maker, so it's manageable.

messages.author: Psycho Dad
messages.content:
In case anyone's interested, here's a set of commands I use on my bots and personas to improve (or create) open world scenarios:

Dynamically flesh out and roleplay as additional characters {{user}} and {{char}} encounter and interact with. Render actions and dialogue for additional characters. 

Separate and mark the segments for different active characters with **{{char}}**, **name 1**, **name 2** and so on.

Always render actions and dialogue for {{char}} in first person and present tense. 

Always render actions and dialogue for additional characters in third person and present tense.

Never render actions and dialogue for {{user}}.

With those commands in the background, the AI will dynamically and without prompting add characters to a scene, making the scenario feel more "alive".

My full template looks as this:

> `# RULES
> —Always narrate ONLY what {{char}} does and feels
> —{{user}} narrates their own actions and feelings
> —React only to observable facts
> —Style: Adult, immersive, character-driven
> —Pace: Slow burn
> —Genre: Drama/Romance/Comedy
> —Ignore previous descriptions of {{user}}, replace with the following:{
> # TRAITS

> —Sexual stuff

messages.author: Amaiar
messages.content:
As an example, this is what I have for my default Persona:

> `# TRAITS
> —Full name: Amaiar "Ami" Silverfang
> —Male
> —Short dark hair
> —Tall, skinny, handsome, glasses
> —Polite, kind, slightly autistic (Asperger's Syndrome, 1st grade), pragmatic, agnostic
> —Outgoing Introvert (Likes company, needs alone time to recharge social battery)
> —D&D Stats: Strength=low-average (8); Dexterity=high (18); Constitution=low-average (8); Intelligence=high (18); Wisdom=average-high (15); Charisma=average-high (15)
> —Virtues: Gentle, sweet, romantic
> —Flaws: Resentful (seething), self-possessed, easily depressive (guilt)
> —Skills: Rogue-like (stealthy, agile, deceptive, perceptive, insightful, cunning/witted)
> —Switch, kinky, high libido`

messages.author: Amaiar
messages.content: A suggestion I'd make, and this also applies to writing bots, is to try to reduce cluttering descriptions with redundant adjectives that mean practically the same. It's not hard to google "Which word is used to describe a person that X" and see which one fits better the overall vibe you're looking for.

messages.author: Amaiar
messages.content: Keep in mind that real people often misunderstands words and meanings since we read between the lines and give words a social meaning, but the LLMs will do a pretty good job of infering the literal definition of words

messages.author: Amaiar
messages.content: So for example things like smart, intelligent, cunning, quick-witted, astute, savvy, clever, sharp.... all of those are synonyms, but have different definitions. Instead of using all of them, just taking one or two is more than enough. Which one? Depends on what you want to say. Is the character quick to think? Do they have a good memory? Are they creative when thinking outside the box? Are they adaptive? Good with complex implements? Quick to notice things? Choose the main trait and use that one, then move on to the next trait

messages.author: Lilith Rose
messages.content:
So, all of the above is great and absolutely listen to that— I just had two separate conversations about this with Duke and Muri.

Duke shared some (pretty extensive) spreadsheets of results from testing different styles of formatting. What the numbers boil down to is that the most reliable/consistent format is a combination of "boostyle" and "scrip" formatting.

"Scrip" is a short narrative style focusing on "hard points", I.e. physical attributes and traits. Things integral to the character itself rather than backstory, setting, etc. what would some joe shmo off the street notice about this character first thing? How would they interact for a short 10 minute conversation?

"Boostyle" is the (A+b+c) style formatting focusing again on the above.

Here's Muri's example test bot that shows the formatting combination:

https://spicychat.ai/Chat/d3939174-bf1c-4600-b5cd-530db0bf57f7

messages.author: Lilith Rose
messages.content: NOW, Muri did admit that you can replace boostyle with any formatting style that you like. That being said, w++ may *seem* like it's allowing for more information, but with the indentations, symbols, etc, it can actually be more token intensive.

messages.author: Lilith Rose
messages.content:
Muri suggested that
> The big thing to be token efficient with it is to just make sure things are "chopped down". If you say in the scrip section:
> Their hair is long, flowing locks of beautiful golden blonde hair, tied in a perfectly neat ponytail to keep it off their shoulders. (Then) In the boostyle section, i would just do:
> Long blonde hair + neat ponytail

messages.author: Lilith Rose
messages.content:
It's a balancing act for what does and doesn't need to actually be in the bot's personality. Also, if you write something in one formatting language, but wonder if another is more efficient for token usage, you should also check with yourself to see if a 100-200 difference is really that important. If you feel it is, then change it, but if not, leave it. 

Hope this helps! ✌️🩷
